stories.summary: While recording an episode with the writer Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand's granddaughter, Amit noticed that her childhood memories were so precise and evocative they read like crafted fiction. He asked how she remembered so much. Her answer was that there was nothing else to do, so they looked at things. Amit extends this to his own 70s-80s childhood: no scrolling or swiping, plenty of empty time, and lots of daydreaming.
stories.insight: Deep observation and rich memory grow out of unclaimed time. When time was the one thing not in short supply, attention settled on the world. Today that has to be a deliberate effort.
stories.quote: And I said, Sara how do you remember so much? And she was like, we had nothing else to do. So we looked at things.

stories.topic: Mixtapes for the Girl He Was Wooing
stories.summary: Amit pulls out a TDK and a Sony cassette he filled with music at nineteen for a seventeen-year-old girl he later married. Making one meant finding scarce foreign music, working a double-deck player with one tape playing and one recording, and calculating how many minutes of songs would fit on a side. It took hours and couldn't be sped up. He made mixtapes for friends too, and claims a 100% strike rate with the people he was wooing.
stories.insight: A mixtape sent two messages. To the recipient it said 'this is who I am, and I want you to like it.' To the maker, choosing what you love and why was itself a way of shaping who you are. A one-minute Spotify playlist carries neither message.
stories.quote: You are sharing a part of yourself. You are basically saying to them, at one hand, this is who I am, and at the other hand, that I want you to like this, right?

stories.topic: Meeting His Younger Self in an Old Letter
stories.summary: Amit found a long letter he had once written, though he doesn't remember to whom. It sketched the plot of a story he was planning. He usually remembers his younger self as shallow and unlikeable, but the letter showed an interesting person he hadn't expected.
stories.insight: Written records challenge the stories we tell about our past selves. Without them, our memory of who we were may be unfairly filtered.
stories.quote: So my memories of myself, the younger me, tend to be very shallow and kinda negative. I don't like who I was.

stories.topic: Posting Letters to a Friend Two Buildings Away
stories.summary: In Class 8, Ajay and his friend Manisha Purohit sat a desk apart at school and lived two buildings apart in Bandra East. They still started a ritual of writing letters to each other and dropping them in the post box.
stories.insight: Writing is a different register from talking. A letter written with care and read with care carries a quality of attention that daily closeness doesn't supply.
stories.quote: Just you're living two buildings away. But it's a delight to write and get those physical pieces of paper

stories.topic: CMIE Was Born in a Stack of Inland Letters
stories.summary: On 13 April 1976, Ajay's father came home and said he had been sacked. Asked what he would do, he said he would start a new organisation called CMIE. That same evening he wrote inland letters to friends all over India explaining what had happened, what he planned, and what help he needed from each of them.
stories.insight: Institutions start in trust networks. The founding act was a burst of careful, personal, specific asks, written by hand on the night of a setback.
stories.quote: CMIE got started with handwritten inland letters sent out to friends all over the country

stories.topic: The Locked Almirah and Dad's 1967 Playboys
stories.summary: Every Godrej steel almirah in Amit's childhood home was left unlocked except the one in his father's study. As a boy he found the hidden key and opened it. Among video cassettes and books were Playboy and Mayfair magazines. He brings two Playboys from May and November 1967, when his father was 25-26. Before Indian magazines like Debonair existed, this was nearly the only window into sex. Amit adds that Playboy was also a serious literary venue.
stories.insight: Scarcity shaped the imagination of a whole generation. The same magazine also held some of the best short fiction and long-form journalism of its time, so the line between highbrow and lowbrow was never as neat as we assume.
stories.quote: There is something I'm not supposed to see and therefore I must see it.

stories.summary: Amit's father, a government servant, got free diaries every year and passed them on because he knew his son wanted to be a writer: 'Beta, likho.' In the 1986 diary, twelve-year-old Amit began a novel called 'Tales of Saint Johns', Part One, Chapter One: 'Tantalising Tantrums'. He wrote a couple of chapters and then stopped. He now sees the mostly empty diary as a symbol of all the writing he hasn't done.
stories.insight: Simply having paper was a privilege he took for granted. Many children never had enough pages to write badly and often, which is how anyone gets good.
stories.quote: And it's actually a sign of great privilege. Great luck that you even have the space to be able to write in something.

stories.topic: The Address Book as Everyone You Know
stories.summary: Amit shows an old household address book. It was nominally alphabetical but really chaotic, with numbers scribbled at the front and back and slips of paper shoved in. It sat in a fixed spot in the home and held everyone: relatives with their postal addresses, friends, the grocer, the electrician, the plumber. Ajay remembers his sister Sadna, who had very high standards of organisation, copying the chaos into a fresh diary every few years, only for it to turn chaotic again.
stories.insight: A physical book of contacts made your social world visible and kept reminding you to tend it. Our phones hold more contacts but leave us less aware of whom we've let drift.
stories.quote: You can pick this up and say, these are all the people I know. Now we can't do that.

stories.summary: Ajay passes on a friend's idea of 'one-way journeys': for most of history, when someone left, you didn't know whether they'd arrive safely, return, or ever be seen again. There were no phones, letters barely worked, and shipwrecks were real. Today video calls are everywhere and flying is easy, so nobody truly leaves. Amit links this to the old Hindu injunction against overseas travel. He reads it as elders afraid that the young would go and never come back, since even Bombay to Kanpur could once take a month.
stories.insight: Technology has quietly retired a whole emotional category: the goodbye that might be final. Some religious rules make more sense when read as defences against that old fear.
stories.quote: So it's a very different thing what was happening in the olden days where People left and there were discontinuous disruptions of relationships.

stories.summary: Amit's mother died of pancreatic cancer in 2008. Knowing she would go, she carefully wrote down recipes for all the dishes he loved, including a favourite liver recipe, and gave them to him. When he cleared out his father's house, he also found his maternal grandmother's recipe book from the 1960s. It was written in beautiful English and mixed Western and Indian dishes.
stories.insight: Handwritten recipes record love and inner lives. For his grandmother, a woman constrained by her world, cooking was a rich creative space, not just drudgery. Today's flood of free YouTube recipes can't hold that kind of meaning.
stories.quote: She knew she was going to go. So before she went, she painstakingly wrote down recipes of all the stuff I liked and gave it to me.

stories.topic: A Recipe Book Compiled by Code
stories.summary: As a PhD student who had to cook, Ajay and Susan built their own system. They wrote each recipe as a text file in a fixed format, and an AWK program converted it into LaTeX, producing a PDF recipe book.
stories.insight: Each generation stores its family knowledge in its own medium. Ajay's version is the engineer's answer to the grandmother's handwritten notebook.
stories.quote: Susan and I built the following machinery that we invented a text file representation for a recipe.

stories.summary: Amit was never the networking type, but at MTV, his third job, he was told he needed a visiting card. Asked for a designation, he found 'writer' too boring and asked for 'Creative Animal', which they printed. After a promotion he wanted a new card, and asked what a step up from Creative Animal would be. He got 'Manic Beast'.
stories.insight: Even a 2-inch card is a small canvas for refusing the default. Amit's titles were a playful bit of self-definition in a corporate setting.
stories.quote: So I said, What is a promotion from creative animal? So I got Manic Beast.

stories.topic: Narendra Shenoy's Half-Hour on Michael Porter
stories.summary: Amit retells a story from his episode with Narendra Shenoy. Narendra had an arranged marriage with Sheila, whose twin sister was paired with a very talkative man. Narendra was not a talker, and Sheila once asked whether he had anything to talk about. Later, studying for an MBA in another city and phoning her long-distance, he felt the pressure to be interesting and spent half an hour explaining Michael Porter's business philosophy.
stories.insight: A scarce, expensive call had to count, and that pressure produced sweet absurdities. The medium shaped what people felt they had to perform.
stories.quote: So for half an hour he tells her about the business philosophy of Michael Porter. So I mean this is what boys were like.

stories.summary: In college, students queued at the yellow STD booths at night to call home. One evening a new student from UP, at the booth next to Amit's, got his mother on the line and opened with a formal 'Pranam, Mataji'. Everyone around turned to stare.
stories.insight: Shared public phone infrastructure put people's private family registers on display. STD booths were small stages where different cultures bumped into each other.
stories.quote: And everybody's just looking at him saying, What the fuck happened?

stories.topic: One Payphone for a Whole IIT Hostel
stories.summary: At Ajay's IIT Bombay hostel, the entire hostel shared one coin payphone, with queues to make calls. For incoming calls, the watchman answered and heard something like 'I want to speak with Ajay Shah of 262', then went shouting '262!' until the student ran down. Ajay also recalls payphones in New York or Singapore being turned into Wi-Fi points before phones had internet.
stories.insight: Communication used to be a shared, public event in community life. Payphones and the people who ran them were a whole social system that has disappeared.
stories.quote: the watchman would come shouting two six two and then you would run down and pick up the phone.

stories.summary: Ajay's father bought the Survey of India's four-sheet map of India, built a wooden board of the right size, and pasted the sheets into a 3m x 3m wall map. Whenever a place or river came up, the kids would scamper up to look. Ajay has tried for years to build a similar wall map of the Himalayas. He thinks a German company makes a good six-sheet set, and he asks listeners for help finding it.
stories.insight: A big paper map makes geography part of daily life and gives a strategic overview that screens can't, partly because digital map legends aren't designed for that purpose.
stories.quote: which was covered with a map of India, which was sold by the Survey of India as four sheets.

stories.topic: The Badminton Partner Who Needed an Urgent Call
stories.summary: Amit had come straight from a boys' school to Fergusson College and couldn't read signals from girls. A girl he played badminton with rang his doorbell one day, with a friend, saying she needed to make an urgent phone call. She made the call and left. Only years later did he realise it was probably an expression of interest.
stories.insight: The landline era had its own language of courtship, like a pretext to visit someone's home. You could completely miss it while it was happening.
stories.quote: And it took me many years to kind of figure out that this was some kind of expression of interest in some way, because why the hell would you go into a random person house?

stories.summary: Ajay recounts a story from a friend from Calcutta, where the phone system barely worked in the bad old days. Sometimes there was no dial tone, and sometimes you heard other people's conversations. Once she picked up the phone, got wired into two strangers talking, and realised they were talking about her.
stories.insight: Broken infrastructure was everyday reality not long ago, and it could produce moments that sound like fiction.
stories.quote: it was wired together into some two people having a conversation, and it turned out that they were talking about her.

recommendations.item: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (Episode 255 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Sara Rai
recommendations.context: Amit opens the episode with Sara Rai's answer about how she remembered her childhood so vividly.
recommendations.reason: Her childhood memories are so detailed and evocative that they read like fiction, and they show what unhurried attention produces.

recommendations.item: Chandrahas Choudhury's Country of Literature (Episode 288 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandrahas Choudhury
recommendations.context: Amit cites his novelist friend Chandrahas as someone who still writes emails like old-fashioned letters.
recommendations.reason: A living example that long, narrative, memory-rich correspondence is still possible.

recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Ajay brings it up during the discussion of handwritten letters: Nehru's letters to his daughter added up to a book.
recommendations.reason: Ajay places it among the world's great intellectual creations, as proof that careful letters can become literature.

recommendations.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
recommendations.context: Paired with Nehru's book as another work that grew out of letters, here Tolkien's to his children.
recommendations.reason: Another case of a person writing letters that more or less become a book.

recommendations.item: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
recommendations.creator: Edited by Alice K. Turner
recommendations.context: Amit calls it one of his treasured books, bought around 1998-99, while arguing that he really did read Playboy for the stories.
recommendations.reason: It is where he first read Haruki Murakami ('The Second Bakery Attack'), alongside Updike, Cheever, Nabokov and others. Playboy and The New Yorker were once the two prestige homes for short fiction.

recommendations.creator: Playboy (interview with Larry Page and Sergey Brin)
recommendations.context: Ajay adds it when Amit describes Playboy's serious content.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that the magazine ran substantive long-form interviews with major figures.

recommendations.item: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
recommendations.creator: Robin Dunbar
recommendations.context: Amit mentions that Dunbar has a book on Dunbar's number while describing the old address book as 'Dunbar plus'.
recommendations.reason: It explains why our brains are built to track about 150 people, with a few close friends at the core, which is useful for being intentional about relationships.

recommendations.creator: Neil Young
recommendations.context: During the 'one-way journeys' segment, Ajay's 'I was thinking about what a friend once said' is echoed by the line 'I was hoping it was a lie', and the song is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Its lyric fits the conversation about a friend's idea of journeys from which people may never return.

recommendations.creator: Wah Chef
recommendations.context: While contrasting handwritten family recipe books with today's endless YouTube recipes, Amit names his favourite.
recommendations.reason: His personal favourite cooking video, which he promised to link.

recommendations.item: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Narendra Shenoy
recommendations.context: The source of the STD-booth story about Narendra explaining Michael Porter to his future wife.
recommendations.reason: The full conversation behind one of the episode's most charming anecdotes.

recommendations.item: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it after the STD-booth stories, noting that mobile roaming wiped out an industry employing millions.
recommendations.reason: A concrete Indian case that job losses from technological change usually aren't a crisis in a dynamic market economy, because people move on to other work.

recommendations.item: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Ajay laments the loss of paper maps.
recommendations.reason: Their earlier full-length conversation on maps.

recommendations.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Borges in response to Ajay's hunt for a perfect wall map of the Himalayas.
recommendations.reason: Borges's idea that a fully accurate map must be as big as the territory, used as a witty reminder that all maps compress.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: Brought up through the answering-machine discussion.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, ranking the Beatles' album second.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions answering machines connected to landlines and Amit recalls this song.
recommendations.reason: Its line 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?' carries a pathos that a generation without answering machines won't feel.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vitalik Buterin
recommendations.context: Ajay cites what Vitalik told them in Madras while making the closing case for cash.
recommendations.reason: The conversation where they discussed how much we lose when cash's universal acceptance breaks down and every transaction becomes traceable.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit describes how the course asks participants to journal daily on a given subject, privately, without showing it to anyone.
recommendations.reason: It puts into practice the episode's claim that writing shapes you, and private journaling lets you think unfiltered.

recommendations.item: The tweet that inspired this episode
recommendations.creator: @NoContextHumans
recommendations.context: Amit opens by citing a tweet asking what has gradually disappeared over the last twenty years without anyone noticing.
recommendations.reason: The question that set off the whole conversation about lost objects.

core_ideas.concept: We Shape Our Objects, Then Our Objects Shape Us
core_ideas.explanation: An object is never just its function. Behaviours, rituals and culture grow up around it. When the object vanishes, that whole world goes with it, so the loss is more than functional. That is why the hosts treat lost objects as lessons rather than nostalgia.
core_ideas.quote: But the entire world we built around the older object is something that we should reflect more upon.

core_ideas.explanation: Each of these objects left our lives without us noticing the final time we used it. Ajay suggests trying to stay aware, in the present, that some everyday act may be your last one with a given thing.
core_ideas.quote: Imagine if you could recall with each of these objects that this is the last time I did X.

core_ideas.concept: Time Was the One Thing Not Scarce
core_ideas.explanation: In the 70s and 80s, books, music and films were scarce but free time was plentiful. Empty time led to daydreaming and close observation. Today's endless stream of stimulation keeps us in a shallow rhythm, and depth now takes deliberate effort. Amit frames this as a lament about himself, not a complaint about kids.
core_ideas.quote: Because the one scarcity that was not so acute as today was time.

core_ideas.explanation: Mixtapes, letters and once-a-week calls demanded time and focus, and that effort both signalled care and formed the person doing it. Too much easy access erodes that focus. The point is not that friction is good in itself. It is that the old friction forced attention, and now we have to choose it.
core_ideas.quote: We claim that by demanding effort and attention and focus, we harnessed the CPU seconds of the mind into doing this and that created beauty

core_ideas.explanation: Following Joan Didion's line 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', writing is how we discover ourselves and our ideas, not just how we report them. Handwriting goes further: it is slower, gives physical feedback, and is hard to edit, so it demands more thought. Amit notes that historians can read Nehru's and Patel's letters, while today's leaders leave almost no letters behind.
core_ideas.quote: when you write, you're not only expressing yourself, you are shaping yourself.

core_ideas.concept: Email Can Still Be a Letter
core_ideas.explanation: Email doesn't have to be quick and careless. You can treat it as an essay: keep it in drafts, edit for days, and flag it with a subject like 'long form...'. Ajay and Lant Pritchett exchange 3,000-word emails, take a month to reply, and expect the exchange to run for years.
core_ideas.quote: You can edit it for days and you can make it a great essay.

core_ideas.concept: Asynchronous Messaging Is a New Frame of Mind
core_ideas.explanation: Communication used to be either nothing or synchronous: you lined up at a booth and spoke live. Async text created a third mode with its own psychology, and it pushed the bar for what is worth sending down to zero. Amit adds that being able to reach anyone anytime removes the urgency to stay in touch at all.
core_ideas.quote: asynchronous messaging is a very different frame of mind compared to either nothing or synchronous.

core_ideas.explanation: Dunbar's number says our brains evolved to track about 150 people, roughly a tribe, with around five close friends and a wider circle of perhaps twenty. The old address book held that circle plus the grocer, electrician and plumber, all in one physical place. Seeing it constantly reminded you whom to keep in touch with. Without that, unintentional neglect lets relationships drift.
core_ideas.quote: This is a physical manifestation of all the people you know in the world with their phone numbers.

core_ideas.concept: Religious Injunctions Reflect a Society's Fears
core_ideas.explanation: Amit suggests that many religious rules encode practical worries of their time. Avoiding pork guarded against disease from improperly cleaned meat. Forbidding overseas travel may have kept the young from disappearing on one-way journeys.
core_ideas.quote: religions, in a sense, among the many functions that they perform, they reflect the mores of a society.

core_ideas.concept: Getting Good Requires Volume, and Volume Requires Paper
core_ideas.explanation: You get better at writing through sheer repetition, writing so much that most of it can be thrown away. For many families, spare notebooks were a luxury beyond school needs, so simply having pages to write in was a privilege. Scarcity cuts both ways: a precious diary can motivate, but it can also paralyse you into letting perfection become the enemy of production.
core_ideas.quote: if you don't have a large enough sample size, you don't get enough iterations in you don't get good.

core_ideas.concept: Creative Destruction: The STD Booth Lesson
core_ideas.explanation: Mobile roaming wiped out an industry of more than a million STD booths and their millions of workers almost overnight, yet it didn't become a catastrophe. In a dynamic market economy, displaced workers find other jobs, so gloom about job loss is usually misplaced.
core_ideas.quote: Most of the time in India, job loss is not a problem because there is a creative dynamic market economy and people move on, they get other jobs

core_ideas.concept: Paper Maps Give a Strategic View
core_ideas.explanation: Wall-sized paper maps from Bartholomew or National Geographic were designed for an overview of the world, which Google Maps' legends are not, even on a 48-inch screen. Children today can neither read nor fold a paper map, and a way of seeing the world is fading.
core_ideas.quote: But I think that there is a strategic sense that you see in a paper map that you don't see on Google Maps.

core_ideas.explanation: Cash is anonymous and accepted everywhere: you can walk into any establishment and complete a transaction. A fully electronic world makes you traceable, a panopticon. Ajay points to China, where cash acceptance has broken down, and calls using cash a social responsibility.
core_ideas.quote: Because in a fully electronic world you are now fully traceable and it's a different environment where you know that you are in the panopticon.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's modern replacement for visiting cards is a QR code pointing to a URL for your VCF contact file. Google Contacts checks that URL periodically, so your contact details update automatically in other people's phones.
core_ideas.quote: In the modern world, you're supposed to have a QR of the URL of your VCF file.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay arrives with his voice failing and asks what the big bag is for. Amit: 'I have a new voice for you in my bag, so in case your voice goes... no no, I'm just kidding.'
Amit on mixtapes: he made them for friends too, 'But as far as people you are wooing is concerned, hundred percent strike rate.'
Amit proposes, live on the recording, a newsletter of alternating long letters between the two hosts. Ajay declines: 'But we talk too much. You also need a little starvation of connection.'
Working out that his father was 25-26 when the 1967 Playboys came out, Amit muses that one might have been a twenty-sixth birthday gift, 'coming a little sort of delayed.'
Amit on the old joke: 'people will joke, I read Playboy for the stories. No, the thing is I actually did.'

Editor Nomsita was found reading a Playboy article on psychedelic drugs. Ajay: 'Is she underage for psychedelic drugs?' Amit: 'Nobody is underage for psychedelic drugs. So I've never had any. I'm just saying random things.'
Asked how he got access to such magazines, Ajay says they were in his IIT hostel wing, where 'it was common property.'
Twelve-year-old Amit's unfinished novel opened with Chapter One, 'Tantalising Tantrums', 'which at least alliterates.'
When Ajay admits he never read Biggles: 'Shocking. Your education is incomplete.'
On a late-80s camcorder VHS of himself shirtless and very thin: 'I'm not gonna trust any of you with that precious footage. So it will remain lost forever.'
As Amit describes buying Filofaxes he never used, Ajay tells listeners he was 'thinking about productivity all along.' Amit corrects: 'I'm failing at productivity all along.'
Ajay's PhD-era recipe book, generated by an AWK program that turned text files into LaTeX and then PDF, gets a 'Sashtang pranam', a full prostration of respect.
Amit's MTV visiting cards: 'Creative Animal', and after a promotion, 'Manic Beast'.

Asked how rotary versus push-button phones changed friendship, Ajay says you memorised numbers. Amit: 'Good answer, but not the full answer'. Zero took the most effort to dial on a rotary, so friends whose numbers had zeros were at a disadvantage. 'I'm just kind of kidding.'

Ajay on Calcutta's phone system: 'there is India and then there is Calcutta... everything is worse in Calcutta. What Bengal thinks today the rest of India hopes will never happen to them.' Then: 'Only in Calcutta.'
Amit's music ranking: The Replacements 'had the best album called Let It Be. The Beatles are in second place.'
On 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?': its pathos 'would be lost on the current generation who are like, What the fuck is an answering machine, dude?'
Joan Didion: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', which Amit uses to argue that writing shapes the self.
Ajay's response to Amit wondering where earlier generations even got pens and ink: 'In what furnace was thy brain?', the line from William Blake's 'The Tyger'.
Borges, invoked by Amit on Ajay's quest for a Himalaya wall map: 'the only accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas.'
Neil Young's 'After the Gold Rush': Ajay's 'I was thinking about what a friend once said' is completed by 'I was hoping it was a lie' in the one-way journeys segment.

Shared childhood reading of the era, which Amit says everyone of their generation read because little else was available: Enid Blyton (The Mystery of Banshee Towers, the Five Find-Outers, the Secret Seven), the Hardy Boys by 'Franklin W. Dixon' (a syndicate of writers), Biggles, and Alfred Hitchcock and the Three Investigators.
TV of the 80s: a Televista set on four legs, Doordarshan as the only channel, appointment viewing of Chitrahaar, and occasional episodes of Alfred Hitchcock Presents.
Inland letters, the blue folded sheets Amit's mother wrote to him on and Ajay's father used to launch CMIE, alongside the yellow STD booths and coin payphones of pre-mobile India.
Historians reading Nehru's and Patel's letters, which Amit contrasts with today's leaders, who communicate by email, WhatsApp and '3 AM Twitter' and leave no letters behind.
The panopticon, Ajay's image for a cashless world in which every transaction is traceable, with China as his example.
